strengths: The paper addresses an important and practically relevant computer-vision problem: class-conditional diffusion training on long-tailed data, with explicit attention to both tail-class fidelity and diversity.

CCUA is simple and broadly applicable. The combination of a negative-only representation loss and timestep-weighted conditional–unconditional alignment is demonstrated with both U-Net DDPMs and diffusion transformers.

The empirical scope is substantial: ImageNet-LT at 256×256, TinyImageNet-LT, Places-LT, CIFAR10-LT, and CIFAR100-LT. Reported gains are often meaningful, including ImageNet-LT FID improvements from 33.87 to 25.89 at 40 epochs and from 19.95 to 16.41 at 160 epochs, alongside improved recall.

The component and resampling ablations are useful. On TinyImageNet-LT, either UCL or alignment improves FID and their combination performs best; Table 5 also shows that CCUA counteracts the recall loss caused by resampling.
The paper includes qualitative comparisons, nearest-neighbor analysis, head/body/tail results, computational-cost disclosure, and results under multiple sampling budgets.
weaknesses: The main ImageNet-LT comparison is substantially confounded by batch resampling. Table 1 compares CCUA with resampling against SiT and Dispersive Loss without it. Table 5 shows that resampling alone accounts for much of the 40-epoch FID gain (33.87 to 28.05, versus 25.89 for the complete method). Results against SiT+resampling and Dispersive Loss+resampling are needed at all training budgets; the protocol for other datasets is also ambiguous about whether resampling was applied equally to every method.

The closest long-tailed diffusion competitor, DiffROP, is discussed extensively but never evaluated. Dispersive Loss is compared only on ImageNet-LT, while CBDM and OCLT are evaluated only on smaller, lower-resolution datasets. This leaves the claimed state of the art insufficiently established.

The negative-only contrastive formulation is not technically justified as written. No feature normalization is specified, so its behavior depends on representation norms and can admit scale-driven solutions. The statement that constant embeddings yield the maximum possible loss is false in general, and no evidence supports the stronger claim that the optimum is uniform on a hypersphere. The method also does not specify how token or spatial feature tensors are reduced for the dot products.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The manuscript never reports the crucial loss weights alpha and gamma, their tuning procedure, complete optimizer and learning-rate settings, model configurations, exact CFG search grid, or a code release. It also introduces a timestep weight for UCL on two datasets only, without ablation or selection rationale.

The central claim of improved tail-class diversity is only partially supported. Overall precision/recall is reported on ImageNet-LT, but no tail-specific recall or coverage metric is given. Low-resolution experiments rely mainly on FIDtail, selected images, nearest neighbors, and t-SNE/KDE plots; FID does not isolate diversity, and t-SNE density is not reliable quantitative distribution evidence.

The purported statistical-significance analysis contains only three generation seeds and reports no independently trained runs, confidence intervals, or hypothesis tests. Consequently, it measures sampling variability rather than training robustness, which is particularly problematic for the modest CIFAR improvements.

The conditional–unconditional alignment motivation remains largely qualitative. Figure 11 illustrates similarity for one trajectory, but there is no quantitative timestep analysis, comparison of alternative weighting schedules or cutoffs, or measurement of whether alignment reduces class controllability. Calling a balanced-data DDPM a theoretical upper bound is also unjustified, especially because CCUA sometimes surpasses it.

strengths: The problem of class-imbalanced conditional image generation is relevant, and improving tail-class diversity without degrading head classes would be valuable.
CCUA is conceptually simple and can be attached to both U-Net DDPM and transformer-based SiT architectures without adding inference-time cost.
The empirical scope is reasonably broad: ImageNet-LT, TinyImageNet-LT, Places-LT, CIFAR10-LT, and CIFAR100-LT are evaluated using FID, tail FID, KID, precision, recall, and qualitative comparisons.

The component ablation suggests that both the contrastive and conditional-unconditional alignment losses contribute. The reported ImageNet-LT improvements, especially in FID and recall, are substantial.
The paper acknowledges the additional training cost and supplies useful qualitative nearest-neighbor and feature-space analyses of tail-class behavior.
weaknesses: No contribution type is declared, so I assess this as Algorithms/General. The central contrastive objective is not technically convincing as written. Equation (1) uses each embedding as its own positive with dot-product similarity, but specifies neither L2 normalization nor another norm constraint. The loss can therefore be minimized by increasing feature norms whenever self-similarity exceeds cross-similarity. The claims that collapse gives the maximum possible loss and that the optimum is a uniform distribution on a hypersphere are false without additional constraints. This undermines the proposed explanation for improved diversity and leaves unclear what the implementation actually optimizes.

The main comparisons confound CCUA with batch resampling. Table 5 shows that resampling alone accounts for a large portion of the 40-epoch ImageNet-LT improvement: FID changes from 33.87 to 28.05 with resampling alone, versus 32.25 with the CCUA losses alone and 25.89 with both. Nevertheless, Table 1 compares the combined system against SiT and Dispersive Loss without matching their resampling strategy. TinyImageNet-LT also uses resampling, but it is unclear whether every baseline receives it. Consequently, the headline comparisons do not cleanly establish the advantage of the proposed losses.

The directly relevant DiffROP method is discussed and characterized as a special case of the proposed approach, yet it is omitted from the experimental comparisons. This weakens the novelty and state-of-the-art case.

The diversity evidence is incomplete. Aggregate recall is reported only for ImageNet-LT, while the remaining quantitative claims largely rely on FID/KID, which do not separately establish improved intra-class diversity. The tail-class t-SNE/KDE, nearest-neighbor examples, and selected image grids are anecdotal and lack systematic class-wise coverage, memorization, or intra-class diversity measurements.

Experimental uncertainty is not properly measured. Results appear to come from single training runs. Table 10 changes sampling seeds for apparently fixed trained models, reports only three FID values, and calls this a statistical-significance analysis without independent training runs, confidence intervals, or a statistical test. It therefore does not quantify training variability or significance.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The manuscript never gives the loss weights alpha and gamma, the searched classifier-free-guidance values or search range, or a precise definition of how the high-dimensional U-Net/SiT feature tensors are pooled and normalized before the dot products. No code availability is stated. These omissions prevent faithful reconstruction of the central method.

The alignment derivation motivates a timestep-dependent KL weighting determined by the diffusion variance schedule, but the implemented objective replaces it with the heuristic factor t/T without analyzing the discrepancy or comparing alternative schedules. Evidence that the gain specifically results from head-to-tail knowledge transfer, rather than generic regularization, is also absent.

Some claims are overstated or inaccurate: a balanced-data DDPM is called a theoretical upper bound even though CCUA sometimes surpasses it; the paper claims head-class quality is maintained despite a slight TinyImageNet head-FID degradation; and the societal-impact statement about underrepresented groups is not supported by experiments on demographic groups. Overall, the promising empirical signal is insufficient to overcome the objective-definition, comparison-fairness, and reproducibility concerns.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical computer-vision problem: maintaining fidelity and diversity for tail classes in class-conditional diffusion models trained on long-tailed data.
CCUA is simple and potentially useful, combining representation dispersion with timestep-weighted conditional–unconditional alignment without increasing inference cost.

The empirical scope is strong: experiments cover five long-tailed datasets, resolutions up to ImageNet-LT at 256×256, U-Net and transformer backbones, several sampling budgets, and multiple generation metrics.

The reported improvements are substantial on ImageNet-LT: at 160 epochs, CCUA improves SiT FID from 19.95 to 16.41 and Recall from 18.61% to 21.34% while approximately preserving Precision. Consistent improvements at earlier checkpoints strengthen the result.
The component and resampling ablations support the proposed design. Tail-group FID, nearest-neighbor visualizations, and qualitative comparisons also provide useful evidence beyond aggregate FID.
The paper is generally clear, appropriately relates the method to CBDM, OCLT, UTLO, and Dispersive Loss, and candidly reports the 1.48–1.6× training-time overhead.
weaknesses: The contrastive-loss definition has a potentially serious technical ambiguity. Equation 1 and Algorithm 1 use raw dot products with the anchor itself as the positive, but never state that embeddings are L2-normalized. Without normalization, the loss admits a trivial norm-inflation solution; consequently, the claims that self-similarity is fixed/maximal and that the optimum is uniform on a hypersphere do not follow from the presented formulation.

The paper repeatedly describes the contrastive term as separating synthetic images, although it is applied during training to representations of noised real samples. Moreover, most negative pairs may belong to different classes. The mechanism by which this specifically improves intra-class tail diversity therefore needs more careful justification and direct measurement.

Evidence for tail-class diversity is incomplete. FIDtail primarily measures distributional quality, while Recall is reported only globally. Per-group or per-class precision/recall, coverage, or memorization statistics would more directly validate the central claim that tail diversity improves without harming head classes, especially on ImageNet-LT.

Reproducibility is limited because the crucial loss weights α and γ are not reported, nor are their sensitivity or selection procedure. The chosen CFG strengths and grid-search range are also omitted, and selecting an optimal strength using evaluation metrics risks test-set tuning.

The statistical analysis varies sampling seeds for apparently fixed trained models; it does not quantify variation across independent training runs. Most results lack error bars or confidence intervals, so the reliability of smaller gains—particularly on CIFAR—is uncertain.

The mathematical development is specific to a DDPM noise-prediction parameterization, but the paper does not adequately explain how the losses and KL interpretation transfer to SiT's interpolant/flow objective. The transformer comparison also excludes specialized long-tailed diffusion baselines, making it difficult to separate backbone effects from methodological superiority.

Originality is moderate rather than high: the two main ingredients closely adapt existing representation-dispersion and conditional–unconditional knowledge-sharing ideas. The demonstrated combination is valuable, but the conceptual advance is incremental. Overall, the strong and broad empirical results slightly outweigh these concerns, supporting a borderline acceptance rather than an unequivocal accept.

strengths: Under the default Algorithms/General contribution type, the paper addresses an important and underexplored problem: class-conditional diffusion training on long-tailed data.

CCUA is conceptually simple and compatible with both U-Net DDPMs and transformer-based SiT models. The conditional-unconditional alignment is a plausible way to transfer information from data-rich classes during early denoising.

The empirical scope is broad: ImageNet-LT at 256×256, TinyImageNet-LT, Places-LT, CIFAR-LT, two imbalance factors, multiple sampling budgets, and both conditional and unconditional generation are evaluated.

Reported improvements are often substantial, particularly for FID and pooled tail-class FID. The ImageNet-LT results are stronger than SiT, CBDM, REPA, Dispersive Loss, and DiffROP, while qualitative nearest-neighbor examples suggest reduced memorization on selected tail classes.

The paper includes useful component, hyperparameter, layer-position, timestep-scheduler, resampling, runtime, and memory ablations. It also acknowledges the approximately 1.3× training-time overhead of the optimized implementation.
weaknesses: The main ImageNet comparison is materially confounded by batch resampling. Table 12 shows that resampling alone improves SiT FID from 19.9 to 16.7 at 900k steps, while adding CCUA improves it further to 15.1. Thus, most of the headline 4.8-point gain in Table 1 is attributable to resampling, which the compared baselines apparently do not receive. The crucial ImageNet tail-FID comparison against SiT plus the same resampling is also absent.

Evidence for the central diversity claim is mixed. On ImageNet-LT at 900k, Recall decreases from 18.6 to 17.3, and under imbalance factor 0.001 it is lower than or equal to SiT at every checkpoint. No tail-specific precision/recall or per-class diversity statistic is reported. FIDtail alone cannot establish that diversity, rather than fidelity, improved.

The theoretical justification for UCL is not sound as stated. Using an embedding as its own positive makes the numerator constant and primarily imposes hyperspherical uniformity; it is not the standard positive-pair InfoNCE setup, so the claimed mutual-information lower-bound interpretation is not established. The chain-rule argument also does not show that conditional contrastive learning admits an identical-within-class optimum, since same-class negatives would directly penalize that solution.

Algorithm 1 samples a separate timestep and noise realization for each image. Consequently, negative embeddings can differ because of timestep or noise rather than image content, providing shortcuts that do not imply greater semantic image diversity. There is no controlled ablation using shared timesteps, matched noise levels, or alternative diversity regularizers to rule this out.

The KL derivation assumes Gaussian DDPM reverse transitions with fixed equal variance, yet the strongest experiments use SiT/scalable interpolants. The manuscript does not justify why the same KL/noise-prediction interpretation applies to that training objective, weakening the claimed theoretical grounding.

The evaluation lacks repeated runs, uncertainty intervals, or significance tests. This is particularly problematic for 10k-sample FID/KID and pooled tail metrics. Hyperparameters and CFG strength are selected through metric-based searches, but no validation protocol is described, creating possible test-set tuning.

The qualitative diversity analysis is limited and potentially misleading: the t-SNE/KDE example uses only five real tail images, and density estimation after nonlinear t-SNE projection is not reliable evidence of distributional coverage. The nearest-neighbor visualization covers only a few selected classes.

Reproducibility details remain incomplete: exact optimizer and learning-rate schedules, model configurations, feature pooling/normalization used by UCL, non-ImageNet imbalance factors, seed protocol, and code availability are not clearly specified. These issues, together with the resampling confound and unsupported theoretical claims, leave the scientific case just short of acceptance despite promising results.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant computer-vision problem: class-conditional diffusion under severe long-tailed training distributions. The proposed combination of unconditional feature dispersion and conditional–unconditional alignment is simple and applicable to both U-Net DDPMs and diffusion transformers.

The evaluation covers several datasets, resolutions, imbalance factors, architectures, and sampling-step settings. The reported FID improvements are generally consistent, including on Places-LT and CIFAR-LT where batch resampling is not used.

The component ablations show that both UCL and AL can improve the SiT baseline, while their combination is usually stronger. The paper also reports computational overhead and includes comparisons at approximately matched training time.
The presentation is generally organized, and qualitative nearest-neighbor examples provide some evidence that baseline models overfit scarce tail examples.
weaknesses: The central theoretical justification is not sound. The proposed UCL uses each normalized representation as its own positive, making the numerator constant. This is a feature-uniformity regularizer, not the usual InfoNCE construction, and the claimed mutual-information lower-bound interpretation does not follow. Consequently, the argument based on decomposing I(h;x,c) does not establish that the method preferentially improves intra-class diversity or avoids the alleged conditional shortcut.

Algorithm 1 samples a timestep separately for every image and the encoder explicitly receives that timestep. The contrastive objective can therefore separate examples using timestep/noise-level information rather than image content. At large timesteps it may also disperse representations based on independently sampled Gaussian noise. No control using a shared timestep, timestep-conditioned negatives, or stop-gradient design is provided to rule out these shortcuts.

The main ImageNet-LT comparison is substantially confounded by batch resampling: CCUA uses it, whereas the headline SiT, CBDM, REPA, and Dispersive-Loss rows apparently do not. Table 12 shows that resampling alone changes FID from 19.9 to 16.7 at 900k steps, accounting for most of the headline 19.9-to-15.1 gain. The fair resampled comparison is relegated to an ablation and does not report FIDtail, despite tail performance being the central claim.

The evidence does not convincingly support the claimed diversity improvement. Overall recall is worse for CCUA than SiT at 900k on ImageNet-LT (17.3 versus 18.6), and it is usually lower under the 0.001 imbalance setting. FID and IS do not separately establish intra-class diversity. Tail-specific precision/recall, coverage, class consistency, or a recognized per-class diversity metric is missing.

The qualitative evidence is selective and sometimes contradicts the narrative: several CCUA grids, notably orange and pizza, contain conspicuously repetitive compositions. The t-SNE-plus-KDE visualization cannot reliably establish distributional coverage because t-SNE distorts densities and distances. Comparisons against the unavailable balanced-data distribution also do not show that the generated variations are semantically valid rather than off-class artifacts.

All quantitative results appear to be single runs, with no uncertainty estimates or significance analysis. This is particularly problematic for the relatively small gains over properly resampled baselines and for FIDtail, whose real tail reference set is necessarily small. The manuscript also does not fully specify synthetic class sampling, real-reference construction, guidance-search ranges, or validation/model-selection protocol.

The KL derivation assumes equal fixed reverse variances but then drops a strongly timestep-dependent proportionality factor and replaces it with the heuristic t/T weight. This is acceptable as a heuristic regularizer, but it does not justify the stated KL-minimization interpretation. The claim that a balanced-data model is a 'theoretical optimal' or 'upper bound' is likewise incorrect, as the paper's own results sometimes surpass it.

Under the appropriate Algorithms/General contribution type, the method has promising empirical signals, but the modest originality, invalid information-theoretic explanation, contrastive shortcut, and confounded/incomplete evidence leave the main causal and diversity claims insufficiently established for acceptance. Code or a concrete release statement is also absent, limiting reproducibility.

strengths: Assuming the default Algorithms/General contribution type, the paper presents a simple and practically useful method for long-tailed conditional generation. Combining unconditional latent repulsion with timestep-weighted conditional–unconditional alignment is intuitive, easy to integrate into existing diffusion training, and reasonably original. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_acl_eccv_cvpr_han_medium_20260919T103820Z/scratch/90ff50cc107e47ad8c6f3743fe954b1c/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The principal ImageNet-LT results are strong: at 900k steps, CCUA improves SiT FID from 19.9 to 15.1 and tail FID from 33.9 to 22.5. Substantial improvements also occur throughout training and under the more extreme 0.001 imbalance factor.

The evidence spans U-Net and transformer backbones, five long-tailed datasets, multiple resolutions, sampling budgets, and several relevant baselines. Results on TinyImageNet-LT and Places-LT indicate that the method is not specific to ImageNet or SiT.

The ablations separately evaluate both proposed losses, batch resampling, latent-layer choice, alignment scheduling, and loss weights. Reporting the approximately 1.3x training-time and 1.18x memory overhead is also helpful.

Qualitative grids, nearest-neighbor analysis, and feature-space visualizations support the claim that CCUA reduces obvious tail-class memorization and mode collapse. The method generally preserves head-class FID while improving body and tail categories.
weaknesses: The theoretical justification is more heuristic than claimed. The mutual-information interpretation of the self-positive contrastive objective is not established under the usual InfoNCE assumptions, and the argument that conditional contrastive learning admits a class-constant shortcut does not rigorously show that the proposed indirect route is preferable.

No results across independent training seeds, uncertainty estimates, or significance tests are reported. This is especially important for the relatively modest gains on some CIFAR metrics and for comparisons involving stochastic generative evaluation.

The evaluation protocol needs greater precision. Each method receives a grid-searched classifier-free-guidance strength, but the search space and selection set are unspecified. Likewise, FIDtail is computed for very small tail subsets without clearly stating the real reference set or per-class sample counts, which complicates interpretation of this key metric.

The diversity evidence is not uniformly favorable: ImageNet-LT recall falls from 18.6 for SiT to 17.3 for CCUA at 900k steps, and it also declines under the extreme imbalance setting at several checkpoints. Thus, the strong fidelity and tail-FID gains are better supported than the broad claim of improved diversity without compromise.

Reproducibility is incomplete: no code-release statement is provided, the selected loss weights outside the main ImageNet ablation are unclear, and full guidance-search and random-seed details are absent. These are correctable reporting issues rather than fundamental flaws.
